extracted.intended_audience: authors, reviewers, editors and readers of Royal Society journals; researchers interested in open peer review practices
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and observed effects of adopting transparent/open peer review (publishing reports, optional identity disclosure, and related open-data policies) in scholarly journals. Focuses on impacts for identity, inclusion, reviewer recognition, review quality and post-publication scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent peer review — publish reports alongside articles
rubrics_metrics.description: A number of journals operate transparent peer review, where we publish peer review reports alongside articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing peer review reports alongside articles makes the review content visible to readers and is described as baked into some journals' identities (e.g. Royal Society Open Science). This practice is part of increasing levels of openness and should be supported by infrastructure to display and archive reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer identity disclosure is optional
rubrics_metrics.description: We publish reviews, but leave it up to the reviewer to decide if they want their identity revealed; reviewers may opt for anonymity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise there are good reasons (beyond concerns about bias) a reviewer may remain anonymous. Policies should allow reviewers to choose disclosure and respect that choice. Publishers may also need to consider safety-related identity concerns for authors (see separate criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise peer review reports as citable scholarly outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: By working with Web of Science Reviewer Recognition, we are now able to recognise peer review reports as scientific outputs by assigning digital object identifiers (DOIs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assigning DOIs makes it easier for reviewers to include their peer review work in ORCID records and otherwise receive credit. Journals should provide mechanisms (DOIs, indexing) that allow reviewers to claim and demonstrate reviewing activity as scholarly contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness increases visibility and can improve diversity/inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The geographical and gender make-up of stakeholders has evolved: we see more non-Western authors, editors and reviewers, and a more representative distribution of genders. Greater visibility that under-represented groups gain by opening up the peer review process can encourage engagement from groups historically less visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine open peer review with active efforts to encourage inclusive engagement. Visibility of identities (when disclosed) can help readers recognise under-represented contributors and motivate further participation, though the distribution may still be far from balanced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open reviews encourage better reviewing practices and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Opening up peer review encourages better reviewing practices: reading what makes a good or less-than-good review helps particularly early-career scientists to write better reviews themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing exemplars of good and poor reviews functions as informal training for early-career researchers, promoting constructive and collaborative reviewer identities. Journals should consider the educational benefit when deciding openness policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness fosters reader confidence to raise queries and supports correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater openness (including open data policies) makes readers more confident in raising queries arising from published reviews or datasets, reinforcing the journals' identities as bastions of scientific rigour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open peer review, coupled with open data, enhances post-publication scrutiny and community-driven correction of the record. Publishers should expect and facilitate queries and corrections as part of an open-process workflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect identity and safety where necessary (author identity amendments)
rubrics_metrics.description: On occasion publishers have amended author identities where authors have expressed concerns that their published identity differs from their 'real' identity and that a separation between the two is sometimes important for the safety of authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies must balance transparency with safety: allow amendments or pseudonymous publication where necessary, and have processes to handle author/ reviewer requests related to identity protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt openness flexibly and evaluate impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Several journals have adopted similar transparent models since Royal Society Open Science launched with this model; the organisation reflects on what has been learnt since switching to open peer review and asks how greater openness has affected identities and the reviews themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement openness incrementally across journals, monitor impacts (on diversity, review quality, reader engagement, and safety), and be prepared to adapt policies based on observed outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complement open peer review with open data policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Open peer review together with related open data policies has the effect of increasing reader confidence to raise queries and enabling scrutiny of reviews and the underlying data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate peer review transparency with data-sharing policies to maximise accountability and enable informed post-publication discussion and corrections.
